A review of whether NoteDown's end-to-end encryption holds what
`docs/sync-and-sharing.md` promises, done on 2026-10-30 before a release in
the Play Store. All findings were dealt with the same day: H1–H4 and M1–M6 fixed (M5
takes effect once the signing secrets are moved in GitHub), L1–L6 fixed or
disclosed (signed news, the fuller answer to L4, is backlog #69). The other docs describe
the fixed state; this file keeps the findings, their status and why.

## Scope and method

- **Read:** the client's cryptography and sync (`app/js/core/crypto.js`,
  `vault.js`, `sync-state.js`, `merge.js`, `app/js/sync/`), how untrusted
  content is rendered (`app/js/core/markdown.js`, the HTML sinks in
  `app/js/ui/`), the server (`server/notedown_server/`: `auth.py`, `app.py`,
  `protocol.py`, `admin.py`, `trmnl/`), the Android shell
  (`mobile/android/`: manifest, `VaultPlugin`, `PrivacyPlugin`,
  `ShareFilePlugin`, `QuickCapturePlugin`) and `.github/workflows/`.
- **Proven, not only read:** H1 and H2 against a local server with the
  app's own modules — a server named in an invitation link got a token for
  the victim's device on the real server, and an older ciphertext uploaded as
  a newer version was accepted and merged, dropping a note; H3 and H4 with
  the app's key-trust code (`openWrap`, `keyVerdict`) on real signed device
  lists and wraps. These scenarios are regression tests now (per finding).

## Threat model

End-to-end encryption has to hold against the server: its operator, someone
who took it over, a copy of its database (`docs/sync-and-sharing.md` →
"Principles"). Besides the server: someone who sends a link or shows a code,
a contact (a member of a shared file), someone holding a copy of a device
that signed out or was removed, and the network (TLS assumed). Out of scope:
a device compromised while in use, and the host that serves the web app's
code (a stated exception, "Principles").

## Findings

| # | Severity | Finding | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | High | The sign-in signature wasn't bound to the server: a token relayed through an invitation link | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| H2 | High | A file's ciphertext wasn't bound to its file and version: the server could roll a file back | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| H3 | High | A device list could be served cut back: a removed device was trusted again | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| H4 | High | A signed-out device kept the power to hand out new file keys | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| M1 | Medium | The safety code is a birthday target | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| M2 | Medium | No Content-Security-Policy | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| M3 | Medium | Prototype URL switches work in the deployed web app | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| M4 | Medium | Inflating a file has no size limit (app and TRMNL plugin) | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| M5 | Medium | The release signing key in every branch build; actions pinned by tag | Fixed in the repository 2026-10-30; the secrets still have to move (`docs/operations.md` → "5. Android signing key") |
| M6 | Medium | The relay message of linking a device isn't authenticated | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| L1–L6 | Low | See "Low" | Fixed or disclosed 2026-10-30 |

### H1 — a sign-in relayed through another server (fixed)

- **What:** a device signed `notedown-auth-v1:<challenge>` for whichever
  server it talked to, and an invitation link names the inviter's server
  (`srv=`). A link on the real web app's address with `srv` pointing
  elsewhere made the app sign in there once the user confirmed the contact
  request; that server passed on the real server's challenge and got a token
  for the victim's device, valid for an hour.
- **Impact:** no note text (the keys stay wrapped for devices), but the file
  list and the social graph (members, contacts, device lists), overwriting
  files and keys, H2's rollback, server-side contacts; with an admin's token
  the whole admin page (a restore that empties the server, news to everyone,
  blocking).
- **Fix:** the signature covers canonical JSON with the server's host, the
  identity and the device (`notedown-auth-v2`); the server checks it against
  the host of the request. Deleting with the recovery key likewise
  (`notedown-delete-v2`). `docs/server-api.md` → "Authentication"; apps
  before level 3 get 426 ("App versions").
- **Tests:** `server/tests/test_api.py` and `test_lifecycle.py` (a signature
  for another server, identity or device, or the old message, signs in and
  deletes nowhere), `tests/crypto.test.mjs`, `tests/api.test.mjs`.

### H2 — a file rolled back by the server (fixed)

- **What:** files were AES-GCM without associated data, and the client
  trusted the version the server reported. The server — or a relayed token
  (H1) with the version history's older states — could upload an older
  ciphertext as the newest version; every device decrypted it and merged it
  against its newer base, which dropped every note added since, silently
  and on all devices. `docs/sync-and-sharing.md` claimed the opposite.
- **Fix:** the associated data is the file ID and the version the upload
  creates, so a state opens only as that version. An older version served as
  itself counts as a restored server and is merged from scratch, which loses
  nothing. Files from before open only on a device that never saw a bound
  version of the file, or merges from scratch, and are uploaded again, bound.
  `docs/server-api.md` → "Keys".
- **Tests:** `tests/crypto.test.mjs` (another version or file doesn't open),
  `tests/sync-state.test.mjs` (`legacyFileAllowed`), `scripts/e2e-sync.js`
  ("an older state the server hands out as a newer version is refused").

### H3 — a device list served cut back (fixed)

- **What:** a client took any valid start of a device list and remembered
  nothing. Served without its removal, a removed (stolen) device was active
  again: its wraps were trusted, and the renewal after the removal wrapped
  the new key for it — likewise a contact's removed device when sharing.
- **Fix:** pins — per identity the length of the longest verified list and
  the hash of its last entry; a shorter list or another past is refused. An
  own append pins at once, so the renewal after a removal only takes a list
  with the removal on it. The own list is kept whole, and what a restored
  server lost is appended again. `app/js/sync/pins.js`, `docs/server-api.md`
  → "Device list".
- **Tests:** `tests/crypto.test.mjs` (`checkPin`).

### H4 — a signed-out device handing out keys (fixed)

- **What:** wraps signed by a device that signed itself out stayed trusted
  for any key generation, so a copy of it (the documented case: a public
  computer) together with the server or a relayed token could give every
  device a key of its own, and read every later change; a generation of
  2³²−1 also blocked every later renewal.
- **Fix:** a signed-out signer counts only for the key a device has already,
  or for a device without one (restoring after the last device signed out),
  which renews that key at once. `app/js/core/sync-state.js` → `keyVerdict`.
- **Tests:** `tests/sync-state.test.mjs`, `scripts/e2e-sync.js` ("Lea signs
  out … and are renewed at once").

### M1 — the safety code (fixed)

- **What:** 20 digits from one PBKDF2 over *both* identity IDs. Someone in the
  middle who knows both IDs beforehand needs two forged identities with equal
  codes — a birthday search: about 2·10¹⁰ PBKDF2 runs, some 60 hours on one
  current GPU, not "too costly".
- **Fix:** each identity gets its own part, PBKDF2 over its ID alone, and the
  code shows both parts in the order of the IDs, so both phones still show the
  same; a forger has to match each real part — a second preimage. Splitting
  alone doesn't help at the same length (two second preimages of 10 digits
  cost what the birthday search on 20 costs), but it keeps a comparison of
  only one part a second preimage, where it was a birthday search on the
  compared digits. So the code also got longer: 2 × 20 digits, about 2⁸⁴
  SHA-256 computations to forge (decided over 2 × 30 digits, Signal's
  length, about 2¹¹⁷, which is harder to read out on a call).
  `docs/sync-and-sharing.md` → "Contacts".
- **Tests:** `tests/crypto.test.mjs` (pinned digits, checked against
  `node:crypto`; the same code on both sides; a part depends on its
  identity alone).

### M2 — no Content-Security-Policy (fixed)

- **What:** the escaping of untrusted text (shared notes, news, names) is
  careful — the sinks that carry such data were checked — but it was the only
  layer between a note and every key.
- **Fix:** every page carries a meta policy right after the charset: scripts
  only from the app itself plus WebAssembly (no inline script, no `on…=`
  handlers), no plugins, frames, forms or `<base>`. Inline styles stay
  allowed (markup sets `style="--c:…"`). `connect-src` can't be narrowed to
  the API as suggested first: invitation links name other home servers, so it
  allows https and only the local test servers over http; H1 is fixed by its
  signatures. `frame-ancestors` can't be set by a meta tag (GitHub Pages sends
  no headers). In the Android app, Capacitor injects its bridge before the
  policy or through the WebView, outside it (checked in Capacitor 8.5.3).
  `PROJECT.md` → "Prototype".
- **Tests:** `tests/csp.test.mjs` (every page: the policy, no inline script,
  handler or `javascript:` address); a browser run over every page and the
  main flows recorded no violation; `scripts/e2e-sync.js` runs under the
  policy.

### M3 — prototype URL switches in the deployed app (fixed)

- **What:** `?sample` replaced the stored notes and sync state (one link
  erased a browser's notes), `?api=` pointed the browser at another server for
  good; `?sync=off` and `?platform=android` worked too.
- **Fix:** those switches and `?dictation=demo` work only on a local address
  (`localhost`, 127.0.0.0/8, `[::1]`, private IPv4) and never in the Android
  app; a server an earlier `?api=` made the browser remember is ignored
  elsewhere. `app/js/core/local-address.js`, `platform.js` →
  `prototypeSwitches`; `PROJECT.md` → "Prototype options".
- **Tests:** `tests/local-address.test.mjs`; the browser run above.

### M4 — inflating without a limit (fixed)

- **What:** `DecompressionStream` in `crypto.js` and `zlib.decompress` in the
  TRMNL plugin inflated whatever a member uploaded: a 2 MB file becomes about
  2 GB, so a member could crash the others' apps and, shared with a TRMNL
  display, the 512 MiB server instance.
- **Fix:** a file's text is at most 16 MiB of UTF-8: clients inflate in small
  slices and stop past the limit, and seal no more; the plugin inflates with a
  bound and skips such a file. The file's sync stops with a message, the
  others go on. `docs/server-api.md` → "Limits". Backups and ZIP imports, which
  the user picks, still inflate without a limit.
- **Tests:** `tests/crypto.test.mjs`, `server/tests/test_trmnl_client.py`,
  `test_trmnl_plugin.py`, `scripts/e2e-sync.js` (a bomb from a member, and an
  own text over the limit).

### M5 — signing and CI (fixed in the repository)

- **What:** branch builds signed the preview APK with the release key from
  repository secrets, which every branch's run can read — also one whose
  workflow file was changed on that branch; third-party actions were pinned
  by tag.
- **Fix:** the release key belongs to the GitHub environment `release`,
  which only `main` may use; branch builds sign with a preview key of their
  own or a debug key, and warn while the release key is still a repository
  secret; the web deploy gets only the certificate's fingerprint from a job in
  `release`; every action is pinned by commit. It takes effect once the
  secrets are moved (`docs/operations.md` → "5. Android signing key"). Play
  App Signing, after which CI holds only the upload key: backlog #40.
- **Open:** `server.yml` reads `ADMIN_IDENTITIES` and `TRMNL_CLIENT_ID` as
  repository secrets (low sensitivity).

### M6 — linking a device (fixed)

- **What:** the relay message was sealed for the new device but signed by
  nobody. A malicious server with an identity of its own could, once the
  device was added to the real list, swap the message, so the new device
  joined that identity and its notes and later input went there.
- **Fix:** the link code (v=2) carries 16 random bytes the server never sees;
  the linked device seals them into its answer, and the new device checks
  them before it signs in or reads any list. `docs/server-api.md` → "Linking a
  device".
- **Tests:** `tests/linking.test.mjs`, `scripts/e2e-sync.js` ("a relay answer
  without the code's secret is refused").

### Low (fixed or disclosed)

- **L1 — shared files from strangers (fixed):** "notes are shared with
  contacts only" is enforced by the server alone, so a server someone took
  over could bring in a shared file whose other members aren't contacts,
  under names of its choosing. A file that arrives with no contact among the
  other members is held back as a request (Show / Leave), the acceptance is
  a marker of the private file (`docs/file-format.md` → "Accepted shared
  files"), and a non-contact's name always carries "(not a contact)".
  `app/js/core/strangers.js`, `tests/strangers.test.mjs`.
- **L2 — TRMNL decrypts on the server (disclosed):** notes shared with a
  display are decrypted by the server (`docs/sync-and-sharing.md` →
  "TRMNL"); the share dialog says so, and now the privacy policy too. In the
  Play Store's Data safety form those notes don't count as end-to-end
  encrypted ("Play Store").
- **L3 — the recovery key on the clipboard (fixed):** the Android app copies
  the recovery key and the backup key with the extra
  `android.content.extra.IS_SENSITIVE`, so the keyboard's suggestions and
  the clipboard preview don't show them; a browser can't mark clipboard
  data.
- **L4 — news from a server someone took over (mitigated):** news stay
  unsigned, so such a server can still post; every post now says it comes
  from the operator and that NoteDown never asks for the recovery key in
  news, messages or on websites. Signed news, which it couldn't fake:
  backlog #69.
- **L5 — dictation in the web app (disclosed):** the first dictation in the
  browser says that the browser's speech service gets the recording (Chrome:
  Google's servers), with Continue / Cancel; the privacy policy says the same.
- **L6 — pins without a limit (fixed):** any member could pin every state it
  replaced by flagging uploads as restores, and saved states were pinned
  too; now at most 10 pinned states per file, the oldest beyond that thins
  like any state (`docs/server-api.md` → "Version history"). Authenticated
  calls still have no rate limit: the history is bounded by thinning and
  this cap.

## What holds

- AES-256-GCM with fresh random nonces; X25519 + ML-KEM-768 hybrid wrapping
  with one HKDF over both secrets and a hash of both ciphertexts and keys
  (libcrux-ml-kem); Ed25519 signatures over canonical JSON, pinned to the
  server by test vectors.
- The device list is a signed hash chain the server can't add a device to;
  wrapped keys are signed and bound to file, recipient and generation; contact
  requests can't be forged (the inviter's fingerprint is in the link, its
  secret never reaches the server); linking commits to the new device's ML-KEM
  key in the QR code.
- On Android: the vault's data key sealed by the Keystore (StrongBox where
  present), no system backup, screen security, incognito keyboard, dictation
  on the device and reminders without note text by default.
- Untrusted Markdown: raw HTML escaped, `javascript:` and `data:` links
  neutralised, media loaded only on a tap by default.

## The claim "at least as secure as Signal"

Files under long-lived keys can't reach it, so the store listing should word
it carefully. There is no forward secrecy: a recorded database plus a
recovery key or device found later opens every state of the version history
and after. The server knows the social graph (contacts, member sets), IP
addresses and times. Accurate: "notes are end-to-end encrypted; the server
stores only ciphertext", with the exceptions web app, TRMNL and metadata.

## Play Store

- Google Play's Data safety form needn't list data that leaves the device
  end-to-end encrypted, readable only by sender and recipient. Notes qualify;
  notes shared with TRMNL, IP addresses and identifiers don't.
- Before the first upload: the signing secrets moved as in M5, and Play App
  Signing (backlog #40).

## Not checked

- That `app/vendor/mlkem.wasm` and the other vendored bundles rebuild to the
  same bytes.
- Every HTML sink of the app (those carrying untrusted data were).
- The hosting settings (Google Cloud, Neon, GitHub repository rules) and a
  built APK.
